You've already built the onboarding flows and the design system. Now you need someone senior to design variations and ship them in React with the same components, ready to A/B test. That's one job across design and code, and we'd run it that way.

Our take: variants only pay off if each one tests a single, clear hypothesis. Five versions that differ in ten ways tell you nothing. So we'd agree on what each variant is meant to prove before designing anything.

Working inside a system is familiar ground for us. For Greptile's 2025 rebrand and design system we built 200+ components with dev-first docs, so we design with the codebase, not against it. Sully called our work "super quick turnarounds," which matters when tests need to ship on a cadence.

How we'd run the 4 weeks:
Week 1: review your existing flows and components, agree on 3–4 hypotheses and a variant for each.
Weeks 2–3: design and build the variations in React from your existing components, set up as A/B test options.
Week 4: QA, edge states and handoff notes so your team can keep producing variants.

We can start within a week.

jobs.applicationBrief:
Boxem sells to Amazon and Walmart third-party sellers, people who live in fees, inventory and shipment deadlines. You want a site with an artist's eye, built on the refreshed designs you already have, in three weeks.

Our take: the art has to carry an idea, not decorate the product. The decision that makes or breaks this is choosing one visual metaphor from the seller's world (the box, the shipment, the margin) and running it through every page, including how logistics and analytics are shown.

We haven't designed for marketplace sellers, so here are our closest analogues. For Bland, we built a deliberately bland persona, and the opinion became the brand. For Sully, we carried their site through the $0.5M to $5M ARR stretch by treating it as a sales-enablement problem rather than a redesign.

How the 3 weeks would run, all in Figma:
Week 1: audit the current site and your refreshed designs, then two creative directions for the homepage.
Week 2: lock one direction, then design the homepage and the logistics and analytics pages.
Week 3: remaining pages, responsive views and a small component set so the site stays consistent after handoff.

One question: do your refreshed designs already set the visual language for the product UI, or should the site define one the product grows into?

jobs.applicationBrief:
A piazza that fills up over 24 days lives or dies on mobile: the scene has to feel richer every day without getting heavier to load. And with an English master due Oct 15 and about 23 languages behind it, the framework has to absorb assets and translations without code changes each time.

Our take: build the main scene as layers driven by one config per day and per language. Each unlock adds a layer and its animated state change. Copy, audio and Go Deeper links come from locale files. Your illustrators keep producing, and new assets drop straight in.

Our closest proof is build-side rather than campaign work. For Greptile's 2025 rebrand and design system we built 200+ components with dev-first docs, and their team reported shipping about 40% faster. Sully called out our "super quick turnarounds".

How we'd run it:
Days 1–2: confirm the technical architecture with the publishing team (hosted vs embedded, analytics).
Week 1: the reusable Advent Calendar framework, including date-gated unlocking, revisiting opened days via local browser storage, localisation-ready structure and accessibility.
Week 2: integrate assets as they land, then browser/device QA and delivery.

We can start within a week.

Will the piazza arrive as separable layers per day, or as flattened full-scene states? That decides most of the mobile weight.
